The practical engineering knowledge base for mastering PostgreSQL internals, writing resilient SQL, and operating production databases.

Get Started → Why PostgreSQL? View on GitHub

docs.title: Learning Paths
docs.text:
1. Start Here: Introduction — What is PostgreSQL and core design principles.
  2. Understand Internals: Architecture — Processes, shared memory, and storage layouts.
  3. Write & Inspect Queries: Query Basics and Transactions.
  4. Tune Performance: EXPLAIN ANALYZE and Query Planner.
  5. Operate Reliably: Connection Pooling and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: How to use this knowledge base
docs.text:
Each topic is structured to provide actionable depth:

  • What it is — Clear concept definition and industry terminology.
  • Why it matters — The concrete engineering or operational trade-off it addresses.
  • How it works — PostgreSQL's internal mechanics and execution paths.
  • Practical example — Realistic SQL statements, EXPLAIN plans, or configuration files.
  • Production considerations — Edge cases, failure modes, and battle-tested recommendations.

Version Awareness

PostgreSQL behaviors and parameters can evolve between major versions (14, 15, 16, and 17). Always cross-reference version-specific configurations with the official documentation.

docs.title: Understanding PostgreSQL Connections
docs.text: A PostgreSQL client connection is more than an entry in a connection count. It has a lifecycle, consumes server resources, and can influence concurrency and latency.

docs.title: Why connection pooling matters
docs.text: In the traditional PostgreSQL process model, a client connection is served by a backend process. Creating and maintaining too many concurrent connections can increase memory pressure and scheduling overhead.

docs.title: Practical considerations
docs.text:
• Reuse application connections through a pool such as HikariCP.
  • Set pool sizes based on database capacity and workload, not simply application instance count.
  • Monitor active, idle, and waiting connections.
  • Investigate query latency and lock waits; connection count alone does not explain CPU usage.

Do not blindly increase max_connections

Increasing the connection limit can increase resource pressure. Measure workload, memory, CPU, and queueing before changing the limit.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: Continue with Connection lifecycle and Connection pooling.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: PostgreSQL is an open-source object-relational database system. This section approaches it from a database-engineering perspective: understand the internals, then apply that knowledge to query design, performance, reliability, and operations.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
Area Focus Fundamentals Processes, memory, storage, database objects SQL and Query SQL semantics and transaction behavior Indexing Index structures and access methods Query Performance Planner, execution plans, and tuning Concurrency MVCC, locks, vacuum, and WAL Connection Management Client connections and pooling Administration Backup, monitoring, and configuration Production Engineering Capacity, reliability, and troubleshooting

Recommended order

Start with Architecture, then study transactions and MVCC before moving to query optimization and production operations.

docs.title: Backup and Restore
docs.text: A backup strategy is only reliable when restoration is tested. Choose between logical and physical backup approaches based on recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives, database size, and operational constraints.

docs.title: Logical backup example
docs.text:
pg_dump --format=custom --file=app.dump app_db
pg_restore --list app.dump

Credentials should be supplied using an appropriate secure mechanism, not embedded in shell history or source code.

docs.title: Validate recovery
docs.text:
• Restore into an isolated environment.
  • Verify schema and critical data.
  • Measure restore duration.
  • Document required extensions, roles, and configuration.
  • Repeat the exercise regularly.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Backup and Restore

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Database monitoring should combine workload, resource, and reliability signals.

docs.title: Useful signals
docs.text: Area Example signals Workload Transactions, queries, active sessions Latency Query duration, application pool wait Contention Lock waits, deadlocks Storage Database size, disk usage, WAL growth Maintenance Dead tuples, autovacuum activity Replication Replay lag, retained WAL

docs.title: Starting point
docs.text:
SELECT
    datname,
    numbackends,
    xact_commit,
    xact_rollback,
    deadlocks,
    stats_reset
FROM pg_stat_database
WHERE datname IS NOT NULL;

Metrics should be interpreted as trends and correlated with application and infrastructure telemetry. A single metric rarely identifies the root cause.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Monitoring Database Activity

docs.title: Locking
docs.text: PostgreSQL uses several lock types to coordinate concurrent operations. Many locks are automatically acquired by statements; explicit locking is available when required.

docs.title: Inspect waiting sessions
docs.text:
SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    state,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';

docs.title: Operational workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the waiting PID.
  2. Find the blocking PID using pg_blocking_pids(pid).
  3. Inspect the blocking transaction and application request.
  4. Resolve the root cause; terminate a backend only after understanding the impact.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Explicit Locking

docs.title: MVCC
docs.text: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) allows PostgreSQL transactions to work with consistent snapshots while reducing the need for readers and writers to block each other.

docs.title: Conceptual model
docs.text:
An update generally creates a new row version rather than overwriting the old version in place. Old versions become reclaimable when no active transaction needs them.

flowchart LR
    A[Transaction A snapshot] --> V1[Row version 1]
    B[Transaction B updates] --> V2[Row version 2]
    A -. continues to see .-> V1
    B --> V2

This is a conceptual illustration; visibility depends on transaction snapshots and tuple visibility metadata.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: MVCC is central to transaction isolation, vacuum, table bloat, and long-running transaction diagnostics.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Concurrency Control

docs.title: VACUUM
docs.text: VACUUM reclaims or makes reusable space occupied by dead row versions and maintains visibility information. Autovacuum automates routine vacuum and analyze work.

docs.title: Inspect vacuum activity
docs.text:
SELECT
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    last_vacuum,
    last_autovacuum,
    last_analyze,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

docs.title: Common investigation areas
docs.text:
• Long-running transactions
  • Replication slots retaining WAL
  • High update/delete churn
  • Autovacuum thresholds and cost settings
  • Table-specific storage parameters

Do not disable autovacuum as a general performance fix.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Routine Vacuuming

docs.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
docs.text: WAL records changes before the corresponding data pages are written to their data files. This supports crash recovery and provides the foundation for replication and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: Inspect WAL-related settings
docs.text:
SHOW wal_level;
SHOW archive_mode;
SHOW max_wal_size;
SHOW checkpoint_timeout;

The available settings and operational recommendations depend on PostgreSQL version and deployment architecture.

docs.title: Why WAL matters
docs.text: WAL volume, checkpoint behavior, archiving, and replication retention can affect write latency, storage consumption, recovery objectives, and replica lag.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: WAL Configuration

docs.title: Connection Lifecycle
docs.text: A client establishes a network connection, authenticates, creates a database session, executes statements, and eventually disconnects.

docs.title: Inspect sessions
docs.text:
SELECT
    state,
    count(*) AS sessions
FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY sessions DESC;

docs.title: Questions to ask during an incident
docs.text:
• Are sessions active, idle, or idle in transaction?
  • Are queries waiting on locks or I/O?
  • Are clients opening connections too frequently?
  • Is the application pool queuing requests?
  • Is the database CPU-bound even though connection usage is below its limit?

Connection count is only one signal. CPU, query plans, wait events, and pool metrics are needed to understand workload pressure.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: The Statistics Collector / Monitoring

docs.title: Connection Pooling
docs.text: A connection pool reuses established database connections instead of creating a new connection for every application operation.

docs.title: Application-side pooling
docs.text:
For a Spring Boot application, HikariCP is commonly used as the JDBC connection pool.

spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      minimum-idle: 5
      connection-timeout: 30000
      idle-timeout: 600000
      max-lifetime: 1800000

These values are examples only. They must be sized against database capacity, application replica count, workload concurrency, and other clients.

docs.title: Capacity calculation
docs.text:
A first-order upper bound is:

total application connections = pool size × application instances

Then account for migration jobs, monitoring, administration, background workers, and other services. Keep operational headroom.

Pool size is not a throughput knob

Increasing pool size can increase database contention and CPU pressure. Measure request queueing, query latency, active sessions, and database resource utilization.

docs.title: External poolers
docs.text: PgBouncer can provide an additional pooling layer. Transaction pooling changes session semantics and is not compatible with every feature or application assumption.

docs.text:

docs.title: PostgreSQL Architecture
docs.text: PostgreSQL uses a client/server architecture. A client application connects to the server, the server processes SQL, and persistent database files store the data.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    C[Client application] --> L[Connection handler]
    L --> P[Backend process]
    P --> Q[Parser and analyzer]
    Q --> R[Planner and optimizer]
    R --> X[Executor]
    X --> M[Shared buffers]
    M --> S[Storage]
    X --> W[WAL]

The diagram is conceptual. PostgreSQL's actual process and execution paths contain more components and details than this overview.

docs.title: Main areas
docs.text:
• Processes: server processes handle connections and background work.
  • Memory: shared memory and process-local memory support execution and caching.
  • Storage: relation files, indexes, and WAL provide persistent state and recovery.
  • Query processing: SQL is parsed, analyzed, planned, and executed.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Understanding the architecture helps connect symptoms to likely causes. High CPU may come from expensive execution plans; high connection counts may increase process and memory pressure; slow writes may involve WAL, checkpoints, storage latency, or contention.

docs.title: Database and Schema
docs.text: A PostgreSQL database contains schemas. Schemas organize objects such as tables, views, functions, and types, and provide a namespace and privilege boundary.

docs.title: Inspect schemas
docs.text:
SELECT schema_name
FROM information_schema.schemata
ORDER BY schema_name;

docs.title: Inspect tables in a schema
docs.text:
SELECT table_schema, table_name
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_type = 'BASE TABLE'
  AND table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
ORDER BY table_schema, table_name;

docs.title: Design considerations
docs.text: Use schemas to organize ownership, naming, and access. A schema-per-tenant design needs careful planning for migrations, connection search paths, permissions, and operational overhead as tenant counts grow.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Schemas

docs.title: Memory Architecture
docs.text: PostgreSQL uses shared memory and process-local memory. Configuration settings influence how memory is used, but they should not be treated as a simple per-connection fixed allocation.

docs.title: Important settings
Official reference
docs.text: Resource Consumption

docs.title: Process Architecture
docs.text: PostgreSQL uses processes for client backends and background tasks. The exact set of background processes depends on configuration, workload, and PostgreSQL version.

docs.title: Inspect server processes
docs.text:
On Linux, process inspection can help correlate database activity with operating-system resources. Prefer PostgreSQL monitoring views for SQL-level activity.

SELECT pid, backend_type, state, wait_event_type, wait_event
FROM pg_stat_activity
ORDER BY backend_type, pid;

backend_type is available in modern PostgreSQL releases; check the documentation for the version deployed in your environment.

docs.title: Practical interpretation
docs.text:
• A large number of active backends is not automatically a problem.
  • Sessions waiting on locks differ from sessions consuming CPU.
  • Background workers and maintenance processes have different roles from client backends.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Monitoring Statistics

docs.title: Storage Architecture
docs.text: PostgreSQL stores tables and indexes in relations, represented by files and pages. The storage manager and buffer manager coordinate access to these persistent structures.

docs.title: Inspect relation sizes
docs.text:
SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(
        format('%I.%I', schemaname, relname)::regclass
    )) AS total_size
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(
    format('%I.%I', schemaname, relname)::regclass
) DESC
LIMIT 20;

Use this query with appropriate privileges and validate object names in environments where schemas or tables may be created dynamically.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Installation steps depend on operating system, package source, and the PostgreSQL major version. For production, use the official packages or a trusted distribution repository and define a supported upgrade strategy.

docs.title: Verify the client
docs.text: psql --version

docs.title: Verify the server
docs.text:
SELECT version();
SHOW server_version;

Development versus production

A local installation is useful for learning. Production environments additionally need backups, monitoring, access controls, patching, and tested recovery procedures.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source object-relational database system with over 35 years of active development that has earned it a strong reputation for reliability, feature robustness, and performance.

Core Philosophy

PostgreSQL is designed around correctness, data integrity, and strict standards compliance. Its extensible architecture lets you define your own data types, index types, and custom functional extensions (such as PostGIS, pgvector, and TimescaleDB).

docs.title: What is PostgreSQL?
docs.text:
At its foundation, PostgreSQL is an enterprise-class relational database system that provides:

  • Complete ACID compliance: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable transactions with configurable isolation levels.
  • Advanced data types: Native JSON/JSONB, arrays, ranges, UUIDs, geometric shapes, and custom composite types.
  • Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC): Readers do not block writers, and writers do not block readers.
  • Extensible catalog: Custom operators, aggregates, functions in multiple languages (PL/pgSQL, Python, C, Rust), and custom index access methods.

docs.title: Core Pillars
docs.text: Pillar Capability Operational Benefit Storage & Memory Shared buffers, buffer pool management, OS page cache integration Predictable disk I/O and caching efficiency Concurrency MVCC, row-level locks, advisory locks, vacuuming High-throughput concurrent transactional workloads Durability Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), checksums, point-in-time recovery Zero data loss and dependable crash recovery Extensibility Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW), extensions, procedural languages Easily connects external data sources and workloads

docs.title: Application Architecture
docs.text:
In a production environment, applications communicate with PostgreSQL backend processes through persistent connection pools, leveraging memory caches and write-ahead logs:

flowchart LR
    Client[Application Client] -->|TCP Connection| Pool[Connection Pooler<br>PgBouncer]
    Pool -->|Session| Backend[PostgreSQL Backend Process]
    subgraph Engine [PostgreSQL Database Engine]
        Backend --> Memory[Shared Buffers<br>Memory Cache]
        Backend --> WAL[WAL Writer<br>Write-Ahead Log]
        Memory --> Storage[(Data Files<br>Heap & Indexes)]
        WAL --> WALFiles[(WAL Disk Segments)]
    end

docs.title: How to use this Guide
docs.text:
This knowledge base is organized progressively from fundamentals to production operations:

  1. Getting Started: Installation and environment setup.
  2. Core Fundamentals: Process & Memory Architecture, storage layouts, and schema design.
  3. Querying & Indexing: Query Basics, transactions, and Index Fundamentals.
  4. Performance Engineering: EXPLAIN ANALYZE and query planner internals.
  5. Production Operations: Connection Pooling, backup & recovery, and troubleshooting.

Version Compatibility

This hub focuses on PostgreSQL 14, 15, 16, and 17+. While the architectural foundations remain consistent, always check version release notes for specific configuration defaults and newly added syntax.

docs.text: Ready to get hands-on? Continue to the Installation Guide or explore PostgreSQL's Internal Architecture.

docs.title: Index Fundamentals
docs.text: An index is an auxiliary data structure that can help PostgreSQL find rows without scanning every row in a table. Indexes also add storage and write-maintenance costs.

docs.title: Create a B-tree index
docs.text:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_bookings_property_created_at
ON bookings (property_id, created_at);

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY has operational restrictions and cannot run inside a transaction block. Plan its use carefully during deployments.

docs.title: Choose indexes from workload evidence
docs.text:
• Identify frequent and expensive query patterns.
  • Inspect predicates, joins, ordering, and selectivity.
  • Compare plans before and after adding an index.
  • Monitor index size and write overhead.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Indexes

docs.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
docs.text: EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL intends to use. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual runtime statistics alongside the plan.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)
SELECT *
FROM bookings
WHERE property_id = 1001
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01';

docs.title: What to inspect
docs.text:
Signal What it tells you Estimated rows vs actual rows Possible cardinality estimation error Actual time Time reported for plan nodes Loops Number of node executions Buffers Shared/local/temp buffer activity Sort method Whether sorting used memory or disk

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement

For statements that modify data, execution has side effects. Use a safe environment or an appropriate transaction strategy when testing.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Capture the exact SQL and representative parameters.
  2. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
  3. Find expensive nodes and row-estimation mismatches.
  4. Check indexes, statistics, joins, and data distribution.
  5. Re-test under representative load.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Using EXPLAIN

docs.title: Query Planner
docs.text: The planner evaluates possible execution strategies and selects a plan based on estimated costs and statistics.

docs.title: Important inputs
docs.text:
• Table and column statistics
  • Available indexes
  • Query predicates and joins
  • Cost configuration
  • Data distribution and correlation

docs.title: Inspect planner statistics
docs.text:
ANALYZE bookings;

SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname,
    last_analyze,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'bookings';

A plan is selected from estimates. When estimates differ significantly from reality, investigate stale statistics, skew, correlated columns, and parameter-sensitive behavior.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: Planner/Optimizer

docs.title: Capacity Planning
docs.text: Capacity planning estimates the resources required to meet workload and reliability goals. It should account for peak concurrency, growth, maintenance, failover, and operational headroom.

docs.title: Dimensions to measure
docs.text:
• CPU utilization and query execution time
  • Memory pressure and cache behavior
  • Storage capacity, IOPS, and latency
  • Connection demand and pool queueing
  • WAL generation and replication retention
  • Backup and restore duration

docs.title: Practical method
docs.text:
1. Establish a baseline under representative load.
  2. Identify peak and seasonal patterns.
  3. Forecast data and traffic growth.
  4. Load-test expected concurrency.
  5. Define alert thresholds and headroom.
  6. Revisit assumptions after workload or schema changes.

Avoid sizing from connection count or database size alone.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with symptoms and evidence rather than changing configuration immediately.

docs.title: First-response checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm the impact and start time.
  • Check database CPU, memory, storage, and connection metrics.
  • Inspect pg_stat_activity and wait events.
  • Identify slow queries and capture execution plans.
  • Check blocking sessions and long-running transactions.
  • Review recent deployments, schema changes, and workload shifts.
  • Record the change made and verify recovery.

docs.title: Useful session query
docs.text:
SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    application_name,
    state,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    now() - query_start AS query_age,
    left(query, 300) AS query_sample
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY query_start NULLS LAST;

Be mindful that query text can contain sensitive values. Restrict access to diagnostic output and avoid publishing production query data.

docs.title: Escalation
docs.text: If the database is managed (for example, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL), correlate PostgreSQL statistics with provider metrics, events, logs, and the managed service's documented behavior.

docs.title: Query Basics
docs.text: SQL is declarative: describe the result you need, and PostgreSQL chooses an execution plan.

docs.title: A practical query
docs.text:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS booking_count
FROM bookings
WHERE created_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY booking_count DESC;

docs.title: Logical concepts
docs.text:
1. Filter rows with WHERE.
  2. Group rows with GROUP BY.
  3. Filter groups with HAVING.
  4. Sort the output with ORDER BY.

The logical description is useful for understanding SQL semantics; it is not a promise that the executor physically performs every operation in that exact sequence.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Study transactions and then inspect real execution plans.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction groups statements into a unit of work. PostgreSQL supports transaction control with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK.

BEGIN;

UPDATE room_inventory
SET available_rooms = available_rooms - 1
WHERE room_type_id = 42
  AND available_rooms > 0;

-- Application should verify the affected row count.
COMMIT;

If the application detects that the update did not reserve a room, it should roll back or handle the business outcome appropriately.
